cls: Bronchodilator - short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist (relatively non-selective)
pharm: Sympathomimetic beta-adrenergic agonist with predominant beta-2 activity that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, relieving bronchospasm in obstructive airway disease; less beta-2 selective and longer acting than salbutamol.
quick: Oral: 20 mg three to four times daily; inhaled (MDI): 1-3 inhalations every 3-4 h (max 12/day)
Oral may be taken with or without food; with food if GI upset
Use only if benefit outweighs risk; may inhibit uterine contractions near term
Caution; avoid unless clearly needed - limited data
No specific adjustment established; use with caution
No specific adjustment established; use with caution
No direct interaction; avoid excess (additive tremor/palpitations)
Heart rate, blood pressure, tremor, serum potassium, symptom control/overuse
summary: Orciprenaline (metaproterenol) is a short-acting beta-adrenergic agonist used as a bronchodilator for the symptomatic relief of bronchospasm in asthma and other reversible obstructive airway disease. It stimulates beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, but it is less beta-2 selective than newer agents such as salbutamol (albuterol), so it produces relatively more cardiac (beta-1) effects (tachycardia, palpitations) and systemic adverse effects. It is available as an oral preparation (tablets/syrup) and historically as a metered-dose inhaler/nebulizer solution. The branded inhalation product (Alupent) and metaproterenol products have been discontinued in the United States, and the agent has been largely superseded by more selective short-acting beta-2 agonists; it is not FDA-marketed currently. Common effects include tremor, nervousness, tachycardia, and hypokalemia. It should be used with caution in cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, and seizure disorders, and overuse signals poor asthma control.
indications: Symptomatic relief of bronchospasm in bronchial asthma
Reversible bronchospasm associated with chronic bronchitis and emphysema (COPD)
Prophylaxis and treatment of acute episodes of bronchospasm (inhaled formulations)

dosage.d: 20 mg three to four times daily
dosage.n: Children 6-9 yr or <=27 kg: 10 mg three to four times daily; individualize
Do not exceed 12 inhalations per day

dosage.d: 0.2-0.3 mL of 5% solution (10-15 mg) diluted, up to every 4 hours

admin: For inhaler use, shake well, exhale, actuate during a slow deep inhalation, hold breath briefly, and wait at least 1-2 minutes between inhalations
Rinse the mouth after inhalation; clean the inhaler/mouthpiece regularly
Do not exceed the recommended frequency; increasing need indicates worsening asthma requiring reassessment
Oral doses can be taken with food if gastrointestinal upset occurs
If using other inhaled agents (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid), use the bronchodilator first and follow the prescribed sequence
moa: Orciprenaline (metaproterenol) is a sympathomimetic amine that stimulates beta-adrenergic receptors, with relatively greater action at beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle than at beta-1 receptors, though it is less beta-2 selective than agents such as salbutamol. Beta-2 receptor activation increases intracellular cyclic AMP via adenylyl cyclase, which lowers intracellular calcium and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, producing bronchodilation. It also inhibits release of mediators (e.g., histamine) from mast cells. Its lower beta-2 selectivity and longer duration account for more pronounced cardiac stimulation (tachycardia, palpitations) and tremor compared with more selective short-acting beta-2 agonists.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to orciprenaline/metaproterenol or any component
Tachyarrhythmias and tachycardia caused by digitalis intoxication
relative: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, or other cardiovascular disorders
Concomitant use with non-selective beta-blockers (antagonism) or with MAO inhibitors/tricyclic antidepressants (potentiated cardiovascular effects)
monitor: Heart rate, rhythm, and blood pressure
Tremor and central nervous system stimulation
Serum potassium (risk of hypokalemia, especially with high doses)
Frequency of use as a marker of asthma control

preg: Animal studies have shown adverse effects at high doses, and adequate well-controlled human data are lacking; use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Because beta-agonists can inhibit uterine contractions, use with caution near term.
lact: It is not known whether orciprenaline is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for adverse effects in the nursing infant, use during breastfeeding only if clearly needed and weigh benefit against risk.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established in the product information. Use with caution in significant renal impairment and monitor for systemic adverse effects.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is established. Use with caution in hepatic impairment given altered metabolism, and monitor for excessive systemic beta-agonist effects.

major: Other sympathomimetic bronchodilators - additive cardiovascular toxicity; do not use together except under supervision
Non-selective beta-adrenergic blockers (e.g., propranolol) - block bronchodilator effect and may provoke severe bronchospasm
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants - potentiate cardiovascular effects of sympathomimetics
moderate: Potassium-lowering drugs (diuretics, corticosteroids, xanthines) - additive hypokalemia
Digitalis glycosides - increased risk of arrhythmias
minor: Theophylline - possible additive bronchodilation and adverse effects
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; take with food if gastrointestinal upset occurs.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid excessive alcohol because of additive tremor and palpitations.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause transient decreases in serum potassium and increases in blood glucose; interpret laboratory results accordingly.

emergency: Severe chest pain or palpitations with breathlessness (possible arrhythmia/ischemia)
Sudden worsening of wheeze/breathing after use (paradoxical bronchospasm)

monitoring: Heart rate, rhythm, and blood pressure, particularly with high doses or cardiovascular disease
Tremor and central nervous system stimulation
Serum potassium with high or frequent dosing
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes
Frequency of rescue use as an indicator of asthma control - escalating use warrants reassessment of therapy
counsel: This medicine opens up your airways to relieve wheezing and breathlessness; use it exactly as prescribed
Do not use it more often than directed - needing it more frequently means your breathing condition is getting worse and you should contact your doctor
You may notice shakiness, a faster heartbeat, or feeling jittery; tell your doctor if these are troublesome
If your breathing suddenly gets worse right after using the inhaler, stop and seek medical advice
Tell your doctor about heart disease, high blood pressure, thyroid problems, diabetes, or seizures, and all other medicines you take
pk: Variable; effect duration longer than salbutamol
Bronchodilation lasts approximately 1-4 hours (up to ~4-5 hours)
Store at controlled room temperature; protect inhaler from heat/puncture per label
pearls: Metaproterenol (orciprenaline) is LESS beta-2 selective than salbutamol/albuterol, so it causes proportionally more tachycardia, palpitations, and tremor

The branded inhaler (Alupent) and metaproterenol products are DISCONTINUED in the United States and the drug is no longer FDA-marketed; more selective SABAs (salbutamol/levalbuterol) have replaced it - this record is based on legacy FDA/SmPC and reference information
Increasing need for a short-acting beta-agonist signals inadequate asthma control - escalate controller therapy rather than the bronchodilator
Watch for hypokalemia (potentiated by diuretics, corticosteroids, and xanthines) and hyperglycemia with high doses
Non-selective beta-blockers antagonize its effect and may trigger bronchospasm; avoid the combination
missed: If you miss a dose of the regularly scheduled oral form, take it as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your usual schedule - do not double up. Inhaled bronchodilator is generally used as needed for symptoms.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated beta-adrenergic effects: pronounced tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias, marked tremor, nervousness, headache, hypertension or hypotension, and hypokalemia; seizures may occur. Management is supportive with cardiac monitoring; a cardioselective beta-blocker may be considered cautiously for serious cardiac effects, recognizing the risk of provoking bronchospasm in patients with airway disease.
